findings.evidence: DOM order is #s3-step3 "Confirm your order" (style="order:3"), then #s3-step2 "Enter payment details" (style="order:2"), then #s3-step1 "Choose a plan" (style="order:1").
findings.fix: Reorder the three .step divs in the DOM itself to read Choose a plan, Enter payment details, Confirm your order, rather than relying on the CSS order property alone to establish the visual sequence.
findings.location: #s3-wizard, <div> class="wizard-steps", DOM order of its three .step children
findings.violation: The CSS order values imply a visual sequence of Choose a plan, Enter payment details, Confirm your order, but the DOM presents the exact reverse, so a linearized reading hears the confirmation step before the plan choice or payment details it depends on, reversing the decision sequence.

findings.evidence: The page's only wayfinding elements are the two links inside #nav ("Plan a trip", "Service alerts"); no search form, sitemap link, or breadcrumb trail appears anywhere in the document, and #footer's links ("Privacy policy", "Terms of service") lead to policy pages rather than to related content.
findings.fix: Add a second independent wayfinding mechanism, such as a site search form or a breadcrumb trail reflecting this page's place in the site, so a reader who lands here directly still has more than one way to find related pages.
findings.location: #nav, <nav> element, the page's only navigation mechanism
findings.violation: The page relies on a single navigation menu as its only mechanism for locating this page or its related content, with no second, independent mechanism such as a search, sitemap, or breadcrumb trail present anywhere in the document.

findings.evidence: #s3-customcontrol is a div with no role, no aria-label, no aria-labelledby, no tabindex, and no title attribute, wrapping a decorative img (alt=""); its class name "icon-delete" is the only indication of its purpose and that name is never exposed to assistive technology.
findings.fix: Replace the div with a native <button> element carrying an accessible name, for example aria-label="Delete", or add role="button" plus a matching accessible name and keyboard handling if a native button cannot be used.
findings.violation: A custom icon-only control carries no programmatically determinable role or accessible name, so assistive technology cannot detect that the control exists at all, let alone what activating it does.

findings.evidence: This label alone carries style="color:#cc0000"; the sibling labels #s3-form-topic-label, #s3-form-email-label, and #s3-form-promo-label carry no color styling and no text explains the red color.
findings.fix: Add a non-color signal alongside the styling, such as visible text ("required") or an icon with an accessible name, or remove the color-only distinction if the field carries no special status.
findings.violation: The phone number label is distinguished from every other label by color alone, with no accompanying icon, asterisk, or text stating what that distinction means, so a reader who cannot perceive color has no way to learn whatever status this field is meant to signal.

findings.evidence: The section under #s1-h contains #s1-p1 ("Riders may request a fare adjustment through the mobile app..."), #s1-p2 ("Passengers can check real time arrivals by calling rider services..."), and #s1-img1, an image of accessible-parking repainting; neither paragraph describes an accessibility improvement.
findings.fix: Retitle the heading to describe what the section actually covers, for example "Fare adjustments and accessible parking updates", or move the unrelated paragraphs to a section whose heading already covers that topic.
findings.violation: The heading's wording promises content about accessibility improvements, but most of what follows it, the fare-adjustment and real-time-arrivals paragraphs, is unrelated to accessibility, so a reader scanning headings to find accessibility information is misled about what the section covers.

findings.evidence: #promo carries aria-invalid="true" and its only associated error text, #s3-form-promo-error, reads "Error."
findings.fix: Replace the error text with a specific description of the problem, for example "Promo code not recognized, check for typos or re-enter it."
findings.violation: The error text for the promo code field is present but generic, naming neither which rule the entered value failed nor what the reader should enter instead, so a screen-reader user learns only that something is wrong, not what or how to fix it.
